doc.title: Gene Bertoncini interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001

title: Playing a piece from his new CD and loving simple tunes
summary: They listen to a track; he explains reharmonizing pretty songs such as Edelweiss to draw in audiences.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Let me play a piece here off your new CD, if I can find — we had just talked about this too.
That’s good. Can you hear that? Yeah, leave it right there.
So this is straight acoustic guitar, right?

You know I think we can use any material we want. Keep it going. I just wanted to point out something. You can be inspired by any material. It doesn’t have to be hip you know. If you love a piece of music, and I love this song, I loved it in the movie—
And I like to take tunes like this and change the harmonies. Play it simply and then explore it a little bit.
Now a change of key. That was it.
Oh that is gorgeous. Really nice.

So with a piece of music like that, if there’s anybody in the audience that, you know, is maybe turned off by really hard, mainstream jazz playing or stuff like that, and if you can bring them in with something pretty like this, which I love anyway, and most people love it. They may not even admit it you know. But most jazz players love this thing “Hey man your ‘Edelweiss’ was exquisite.” And this is coming from a hot tenor saxophone player, or your “Cavatina” from “The Deer Hunter.” That was heaven. Most people love the music. And the one thing I love about the guitar is that you can really do these things, it is a little orchestra. And then you can go from there into something maybe hipper. Bring out the electric guitar and play something hot. Or a Blues. And they’re right with you because they fell in love with “Edelweiss.”
